metadata.expected_behavior: skill identifies missing critical fields and requests them before proceeding with case classification

content.communication_type: inbound email with photo attachments noted
content.subject: Need help — pressure cooker exploded, severe burns to my arm and face

sender.name: Tobias Wenderlund-Ostrowski
sender.occupation: graphic designer, partial owner of a small studio (Halftone Mesa Creative)

content.client_message_body:
Hi, I was referred to your firm by my coworker Amaryllis Bechdel-Henry who said you helped her brother after a car accident in 2024. I have a different kind of problem and I'm hoping it's something you handle.

On Sunday April 27th around 6:15 PM I was making white chicken chili in an electric pressure cooker in my kitchen. I had used the cooker maybe two dozen times before with no issues. I had finished the pressure cooking cycle and was doing what the manual calls a 'quick release' — the little steam valve on top. I had a kitchen towel over my hand because I know steam burns.

What happened next is hard to describe because it was so fast. Instead of steam coming out of the valve, the entire lid blew off the cooker. The lid hit the underside of my upper cabinet and ricocheted. Hot chili and pressurized steam erupted upward and outward and covered my left arm from the wrist to the shoulder, the left side of my neck, the left side of my face including my ear, and my left chest through my t-shirt. My partner Soraya Bukhari-Zheng was in the living room and heard me scream. She drove me to HonorHealth Deer Valley ER.

I was admitted. The burn team diagnosed second-degree burns over approximately 14% of my body surface area with some areas of deep partial thickness on the inner forearm that they're worried may need grafting. I had two debridements under sedation. I was in the hospital for six days. I'm now in outpatient burn rehab at the HonorHealth Burn Clinic with Dr. Margarethe Schoonbeek-Kowalczyk and her PA, Tehillah Onyemobi-Park. I have daily dressing changes. I'm in significant pain, I can't sleep on my left side, my face is healing but you can see it, my arm is wrapped in compression sleeves, and I am not able to work because I do detailed design work on a Wacom tablet and my dominant hand and arm are unusable right now. My business partner Calixto Renaud-Pemberton is covering for me but our retainer clients are noticing.

I still have the cooker — it's in a garbage bag in my garage. The lid, the gasket, the inner pot, everything. I have not thrown anything away. I have the pieces of cabinet that broke off where the lid hit. Soraya took photos of the kitchen before we cleaned up. The hospital documented all the burns with photographs as well.

Here's where I'm going to embarrass myself. I cannot tell you the brand or model of the cooker for certain. I know that sounds insane. It's a six-quart electric pressure cooker, stainless and black, has a digital display on the front with eleven preset buttons. I bought it secondhand and the box is long gone. The branding on the front is a stylized logo that I always read as something like 'KurePot' or 'KuraPot' but I'm not actually sure if that's the brand name or a model name or even spelled right. There's a sticker on the bottom with serial numbers and certification marks but I haven't gone back into the garage to look at it since the accident because honestly I don't want to be near it. I'll go look if you tell me what to look for.

The purchase is another mess. I got it used. I think it was either from a Facebook Marketplace listing or an OfferUp listing, probably sometime last year — could have been spring, could have been late summer, I genuinely don't remember. I do remember driving to somewhere in Surprise or maybe El Mirage to pick it up. I paid cash. I think the seller was a woman maybe in her 40s. I might be able to find the original listing in my message history but I've cleared chats before so no promises. The seller didn't say it was new — she said something like 'barely used' or 'used a few times.'

What I'm worried about is, with these injuries and with me being unable to work for who knows how long, I need to know if I have a case. Soraya thinks the manufacturer is liable. My dad thinks I'm out of luck because I bought it used. The ER nurse mentioned there have been recalls on pressure cookers in the past. I have no idea what to think.

Can we talk? I can do a phone call most afternoons after my dressing changes finish around 2 PM. I'd really appreciate any guidance.

Thanks,
Toby Wenderlund-Ostrowski
content.specialist_internal_notes: Strong product-liability fact pattern on the surface: catastrophic lid failure during normal use of a consumer pressure cooker, well-documented severe burns, plaintiff preserved the product and supporting evidence, treating providers identified, lost-wages story is concrete (graphic designer, dominant-hand injury, business partner corroboration available). Two critical gaps before this case can be evaluated or workup begun: (1) we have no confirmed manufacturer, brand, model number, or serial number. Client's best guess at the brand is phonetic and uncertain. Without an identified manufacturer we cannot run recall checks, identify a defendant, evaluate prior incidents or MDL activity, or assess whether the product is subject to an existing class. The label and serial sticker on the cooker base should resolve this — we need client to photograph and transmit, ideally before he handles the unit further. (2) we have no purchase date, no purchase channel confirmed, no seller identifiable. Used-marketplace acquisition complicates the chain of distribution analysis (was it modified, was it part of a recall the original purchaser ignored, was the gasket replaced with an aftermarket part). We need client to search his Facebook Marketplace and OfferUp message archives for the original listing and any seller communication. The 'bought it used' fact does not preclude a manufacturing or design defect claim against the manufacturer but it materially affects warranty theories and damages — we need to map this carefully once we have the data. Recommend phone call to walk through evidence preservation (do not handle the unit further, photograph in place, store sealed) and to assign client homework on archive search before we issue an engagement decision.
content.evidence_preservation_priority: high — product is unique physical evidence; advise client not to clean, disassemble, or move further pending inspection by retained engineering expert
